title: Work and study
job: Explain what you do all day, and how
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE RELATIVE PRONOUN HAS FIVE SHAPES AND THIS COURSE WRITES THREE: quī (masculine subject), quae (feminine subject), quem (object). The neuter is quod — which is ALREADY L1-M9's word for 'because' — and the feminine object is quam, which is ALREADY L2-M9's 'than'. Both are real Latin and neither is written here, because the index gives a surface one owner and a learner tapping a second reading would be shown the first one's note. So the module teaches three cells of a five-cell word and says which two are missing and why.

possum ENTERS HERE AND CLOSES A GAP L2-M8 NAMED. That module said nōn inveniō and meant 'I cannot find', because no level below this one had a verb for 'can'. possum 'I can', potes 'you can', potest 'he can' — irregular, and it takes an INFINITIVE after it, exactly as L1-M3's volō does. The perfect potuī belongs to a later level; three persons and the infinitive frame are what this module opens.

discō IS THE PUPIL'S VERB AND doceō IS THE TEACHER'S, and English inherited both without keeping them apart — 'disciple' is a learner and 'docile' is teachable. So a cognate will not tell you which is which. L1-M1 gave you the two nouns and they are the safe route: a magistra docet and a discipulus discit. lingua is 'language' and also 'tongue', the same double meaning as English 'mother tongue'.

THE RELATIVE TAKES ITS SHAPE FROM ITS JOB INSIDE ITS OWN CLAUSE, and its gender from the noun outside it. liber quem legō: the book is the sentence's subject and the reading's object, so liber is nominative and quem accusative in one breath. English does the same with 'who' and 'whom' and has nearly stopped, which is why the distinction feels optional and is not.

PURPOSE HERE IS ad PLUS A PLAIN NOUN, AND THAT IS A LIMIT WORTH KNOWING. ad labōrem eō is 'I go to work' with work as a place. Latin can say 'I go in order to work' with a shape this course has not taught — the gerund, ad labōrandum — and it belongs to a later level. A learner who wants to express purpose properly is reaching past this module, and the module says so rather than pretending ad plus a noun is the whole of it.

quoque COMES SECOND IN ITS CLAUSE AND NEVER FIRST: ego quoque discō. L1-M10 taught four connectives that must be second — autem, enim, igitur, quoque — and L1-M9 four that must come first, and M1 added three conjunctions that join. The course now has eleven of these words and the only useful thing is the list. There is no version of a sentence where quoque opens it.

words.note: 'Well'. L1-M2's adverb, and it takes no ending — it is the answer to quid agis? turned into a description of how you work.
'To work' — labōrō's infinitive. L1-M4 wrote labōrō, labōrat and labōrant; this is the shape a second verb needs in front of it.
'I can': possum 'I can', potes 'you can', potest 'he can'. Irregular, and it takes an infinitive after it — English 'potent' and 'possible' are the same word.

sentences.trap: L2-M8 said nōn inveniō and meant 'I cannot find', and named the gap out loud. This module closes it: possum is 'I can' and it takes an infinitive, so the thing you can do comes BEFORE it and in the -re shape.
sentences.sound: BE-ne la-bō-RĀ-re POS-sum. The infinitive's long ā is where the stress lands, and the double s of possum is held.

variations.changed: the listener, so possum moves
the negative, which is now available
L1-M7's hīc instead of the adverb

mistake.why: the plain 'I work' where the infinitive belongs. possum needs the -re shape after it, exactly as volō did in L1-M3 — and labōrō possum reads as two verbs with nothing joining them, which Latin cannot do.

sentences.usage: Said about what you are able to do.

words.note: 'Language', and also 'tongue' — the same word for both, as in English 'mother tongue'. lingua as the subject, linguam as the thing learned.
'Latin', agreeing with lingua and so feminine: lingua Latīna, linguam Latīnam. It is the language this whole course is about, and it names itself here for the first time.
'I learn': discō 'I learn', discit 'he learns', discere 'to learn'. It is the pupil's verb, and docet is the teacher's — English 'disciple' and 'docile' split the same way.

sentences.trap: Latin says 'the Latin language' where English says 'Latin' on its own, and the adjective agrees: lingua Latīna as a subject, linguam Latīnam as an object. Two words moving together, which is L2-M3's lesson on the name of the language you are learning it in.
sentences.sound: LIN-guam la-TĪ-nam DIS-cō. The two -am endings rhyme, and that rhyme is the agreement.

variations.changed: both words as a subject, so both endings change
L1-M3's volō with the infinitive
someone else learning

mistake.why: the adjective left in its subject shape while the noun moved. It is L2-M3's error on the two words a learner of this course will write most often, which is why it is worth a plate here rather than being assumed settled.

sentences.usage: Said when someone asks what you study.
sentences.mnemonic: The language and its name move together.

words.note: 'Student' — discipulus for a man, discipula for a woman. L1-M1's word, and it is discō's noun: the one who learns.
'Who, which' for a masculine subject — quī. Latin's relative has five shapes and this course writes three: quī, quae and quem.
'He learns' — discō's third-person shape. The relative is the subject of this verb, so the verb is the he/she shape.
'He works'. L1-M4's verb, and the main clause's verb — it answers to discipulus, not to quī.

sentences.trap: Two verbs and one noun. quī opens a clause that describes discipulus and discit belongs to that clause; labōrat belongs to the sentence. English does the same thing with 'who', and the difference is that Latin's word changes shape for the job the relative does inside its own clause.
sentences.sound: dis-CI-pu-lus QUĪ DIS-cit LA-bō-rat. The relative is one heavy syllable between two long words: it is easy to lose and it carries the structure.

variations.cue: The student who learns works well.
variations.changed: L1-M2's bene added
a woman, so the relative moves to quae

variations.cue: The student who is here learns.
variations.changed: 'to be' inside the relative clause

mistake.why: the I-shape inside the relative clause. quī is a third person — it stands for the student, not for the speaker — so its verb is discit, and writing discō makes the clause about you in the middle of a sentence about someone else.

sentences.usage: Said describing a kind of person.
sentences.mnemonic: quī is a he, so its verb ends in -t.

sentences.cue: The teacher who teaches is here.

words.note: 'Teacher' — magistra for a woman, magister for a man. L1-M1's word, and the other half of discipulus.
'Who, which' for a feminine subject — quae. Its masculine is quī; the neuter is a shape this course does not write.
'She teaches' — doceō, the TEACHER's verb, against discō the pupil's. English keeps both: 'docile' is teachable and 'disciple' is a learner.
'Here'. L1-M7's word.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: doceō and discō are opposite and look related, and English inherited both without keeping them apart: 'docile' comes from the teaching one and 'disciple' from the learning one. So a cognate will not tell you which is which, and the only safe route is the noun beside it — a magistra docet and a discipulus discit.
sentences.sound: ma-GIS-tra QUAE DO-cet HĪC EST. quae is one syllable and it rhymes with nothing else in the line.

variations.cue: The teacher who teaches is here.
variations.changed: a man, so the relative moves to quī

variations.display: Magistra quae docet linguam Latīnam discit.
variations.cue: The teacher who teaches is learning Latin.
variations.changed: both verbs in one sentence, to make the contrast

variations.cue: The teacher who is here teaches.
variations.changed: the two clauses swapped

mistake.why: the masculine relative on a feminine noun. quī and quae are the same word in two genders and the relative takes the gender of what it describes, not of who is speaking — which is L2-M3's agreement on a new kind of word.

sentences.mnemonic: A magistra docet; a discipulus discit.

sentences.cue: The book which I am reading is heavy.

words.note: 'Book' as the subject: liber for one, librī for more than one. L1-M4's word.
'Which, whom' as an OBJECT — quem. It is the shape the relative takes when it is the thing being done to, and it is the third and last shape this course writes.
'I read'. L1-M4's verb, and here it is inside the relative clause with its own subject: me.
'Heavy'. L2-M2's adjective, the same shape for a man or a woman, and it answers to liber.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: The relative changes shape for its job INSIDE its own clause, not for the noun outside it. liber is a subject and quem is an object, in one sentence, because the book is the sentence's subject and the reading's object. English does this too — 'who' against 'whom' — and has almost stopped.
sentences.sound: LI-ber QUEM LE-gō GRA-vis EST. quem is short and closed, where quī and quae are long and open.

variations.cue: The book which I am reading is short.
variations.changed: L1-M7's adjective instead

variations.cue: The book which he is reading is heavy.
variations.changed: someone else reading

variations.cue: I have the book which I am reading.
variations.changed: the book as an object too, so liber moves and quem does not

mistake.why: the subject shape of the relative where the object shape belongs. quī legō would mean 'who I read' with the book doing the reading — and the reason it is easy is that liber is a subject, so the ear wants the word beside it to match.

sentences.usage: Said about something you are in the middle of.
sentences.mnemonic: quem is the one being done to.

sentences.cue: I go to work at the first hour.

words.note: 'To', with the object shape after it. L1-M4's preposition.
'Work' as a THING rather than an action — labor as the subject, labōrem after ad. It is the same root as labōrō and a noun: English 'labour' and 'laborious'.
'At the hour' — M1's ablative, and the ending is the 'at'.
'First', the ordinal agreeing with hōrā. Not M1's prīmum, which is the adverb.
'I go': eō, īs, it, īmus, īvī. L1-M5's verb.

sentences.trap: Purpose in this course is ad plus a plain noun, and that is a limit rather than the whole story. Latin can say 'I go in order to work' with a shape this course has not taught — the gerund, ad labōrandum — and it belongs to a later level. Here the work is a place you go to.
sentences.sound: ad la-BŌ-rem HŌ-rā PRĪ-mā E-ō. The noun and the two time words all end on a long vowel.

variations.changed: the time dropped

variations.cue: He goes to work at the first hour.
variations.changed: someone else
the noun as a subject, which is where labor's own shape shows

mistake.why: the verb used where the noun belongs. labōrō is 'I work' and labōrem is 'work' the thing — ad takes a noun, and a preposition with a verb after it is not a sentence Latin can read.

sentences.mnemonic: labōrō is doing it; labōrem is the thing.

words.note: 'Duty, office, job' — what you owe and what you do, in one word. It is neuter, so it does not change between subject and object. English 'official' and 'officious' come from it.
'Heavy, hard' — L2-M2's gravis in its NEUTER shape, agreeing with officium. Its comparative gravius is neuter too, and shows no gender at all. Of work it means demanding rather than serious.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: officium is NEUTER, so grave rather than gravis. Three levels have taught gravis as the shape that serves a man or a woman alike, and the neuter is the one cell of that word that does move — and nothing about a job is obviously neither male nor female, which is why this gender catches people.
sentences.sound: of-FI-ci-um GRA-ve EST. Both of the first two words end in a short vowel: the line is light for what it says.

variations.changed: a masculine noun, so gravis comes back
the negative
L2-M9's comparative, which shows no gender at all

mistake.why: the two-gender shape on a neuter noun. gravis is right for a man, a woman and nothing else, and officium needs grave — this is the one place M2's adjective family bends, and a learner who has been told for two levels that gravis never moves will not expect it.

sentences.mnemonic: A neuter noun pulls gravis to grave.

words.note: 'Language' as the thing learned. lingua as the subject, linguam as the object.
'Latin', agreeing with linguam and so in the object shape too.
'To learn' — discō's infinitive, and the shape possum needs after it. discō, discit, discere.
'Not', in front of what it denies. L1-M3's word.
'I can': possum, potes, potest. Irregular, and it takes an infinitive.

sentences.trap: Five words in one clause and the verb is last. The infinitive and its own object come first, then the negative, then possum — so nothing tells you the sentence is about ability until it ends. That order is normal Latin and it is what makes long sentences feel unreadable at first.
sentences.sound: LIN-guam la-TĪ-nam DIS-ce-re nōn POS-sum. Nine syllables and only three long vowels: the line moves quickly to its verb.

variations.changed: the negative dropped
the listener
L1-M3's volō, which takes the same shape after it

mistake.why: nōn moved in front of the infinitive. It denies whatever it stands before, so this says 'I am able to not-learn Latin' — which is a real thing to be able to do and not what the sentence means. The negative belongs with the verb that carries the ability.

sentences.usage: Said giving up, or fishing for encouragement.
sentences.mnemonic: nōn goes with the verb that can.

sentences.display: Discipula quae linguam discit officium habet.
sentences.cue: The student who is learning the language has a job.
sentences.literal: student who language she-learns duty she-has

words.note: 'Student', a woman — discipulus for a man. L1-M1's word.
'Who' for a feminine subject. It takes the gender of discipula and the subject shape because it is the subject of discit.
'Language' as the thing learned, inside the relative clause.
'She learns' — discō's third-person shape, answering to quae.
'Duty, job' — neuter, so it looks the same as a subject and as an object. Here it is the object of habet.
'She has' — habeō, habēs, habet. L1-M1's verb, and the main clause's.

sentences.trap: Six words, two clauses, two verbs and one subject. The relative clause has its own object (linguam) and its own verb (discit) and sits INSIDE the sentence; officium and habet belong to the sentence around it. Finding where the clause ends is the only hard part, and Latin gives you no punctuation to help.
sentences.sound: dis-CI-pu-la QUAE LIN-guam DIS-cit of-FI-ci-um HA-bet. Twelve syllables — the longest line in the module, and every word is one you know.

variations.display: Discipulus quī linguam discit officium habet.
variations.cue: The student who is learning the language has a job.
variations.changed: a man, so two words move

variations.display: Discipula quae linguam discit hīc est.
variations.cue: The student who is learning the language is here.
variations.changed: a shorter main clause

variations.display: Discipula quae officium habet linguam discit.
variations.cue: The student who has a job is learning the language.
variations.changed: the two clauses swapped, which swaps what is being described

mistake.display: Discipula quae linguam discit officium habēs.
mistake.why: the you-shape on the main verb. The subject is discipula and habet is its verb; habēs pulls the sentence onto the listener halfway through, and the length is what makes it possible — by the sixth word the subject is four words behind you.

sentences.mnemonic: Find the relative's verb, then the sentence's.

sentences.display: Linguam Latīnam discere potes; ego quoque discō.
sentences.cue: You can learn Latin; I am learning too.
sentences.literal: language Latin to-learn you-can I also I-learn

words.note: 'Language' as the thing learned.
'Latin', agreeing with linguam.
'To learn' — discō's infinitive, after potes.
'You can' — possum's you-shape: possum, potes, potest. Irregular all the way through.
'I' — and discō already says it. L1-M10's row, here for the contrast between two people, which is the one job a pronoun has.
'Also', and it comes SECOND in its clause — never first. L1-M10's word, and one of four connectives in this course that must be second.
'I learn': discō, discit, discere.

sentences.trap: quoque comes second and there is no choosing. L1-M10 taught four connectives that must be second (autem, enim, igitur, quoque) and L1-M9 four that must be first — and ego quoque is a fixed order, not a preference: quoque quoque ego is not Latin.
sentences.sound: LIN-guam la-TĪ-nam DIS-ce-re PO-tes; E-go QUO-que DIS-cō. Two clauses, one long and one short, and the short one carries the point.

variations.display: Linguam Latīnam discere potes; ego quoque.
variations.cue: You can learn Latin; so am I.
variations.changed: the second verb dropped, which Latin allows once it is understood

variations.display: Linguam Latīnam discere possum; tū quoque potes.
variations.cue: I can learn Latin; you can too.
variations.changed: the two people swapped
no second clause, and no contrast to make

mistake.display: Linguam Latīnam discere potes; quoque ego discō.
mistake.why: quoque put first, on the English model of 'also I'. It must come second in its clause and there is no version of this sentence where it opens one — which is the kind of rule a learner only believes after seeing it broken.

comprehensionPool.cue: The student who learns works well.
The teacher who teaches is here.
The book which I am reading is short.
